system_overview: This specification defines and compares five different ways to compute the transitive closure of a binary relation. A relation is modeled as a set of ordered pairs, and the transitive closure is the smallest relation containing the original that is closed under transitivity. The module is a purely definitional specification with no state machine -- it defines operators and uses assumptions to verify their equivalence for small inputs.
actors_and_components: There are no concurrent actors or processes. The module defines a collection of mathematical operators: a support operator that extracts all elements appearing in a relation, a path-based transitive closure definition, a bounded-path variant suitable for finite evaluation, a relation composition operator, an iterative closure using repeated composition, a fixed-point closure using repeated squaring, an operator based on Warshall's algorithm that processes nodes one at a time, and a variant that works with boolean-valued operator representations of relations rather than sets of pairs.
state_variables: There are no state variables. This is a constant-level specification with no state transitions.
initial_state: NOT_SPECIFIED -- there is no state machine.
actions: NOT_SPECIFIED -- there is no state machine. The module defines five transitive closure operators with different computational approaches: (1) A path-based definition using sequences of arbitrary length -- not directly evaluable because it quantifies over an infinite set. (2) A bounded-path variant that restricts path lengths to at most the number of elements in the support plus one, making it evaluable for finite relations but inefficient. (3) An iterative approach that starts with the original relation and repeatedly composes it with itself, accumulating new pairs until the number of iterations equals one less than the support size. (4) A fixed-point approach using repeated squaring (composing the accumulated relation with itself) that converges in logarithmically many steps. (5) A Warshall's algorithm variant that processes each element in the support, adding shortcut pairs through that element, which is asymptotically the most efficient approach. A sixth operator handles the case where relations are represented as boolean-valued operators on a given set rather than as sets of pairs.
safety_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED -- there is no state machine.
liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED -- there is no state machine.
model_bounds: The equivalence of the four set-based definitions is verified by exhaustive checking over all possible relations on sets of size 0 through 3 (all subsets of the Cartesian product of 1..N with 1..N for N in 0..3). The operator-based definition is similarly checked against the bounded-path definition for the same range.
additional_assumptions: The first definition (using unbounded sequences) cannot be evaluated by a model checker because it quantifies over an infinite set. All other definitions are designed to be evaluable for finite relations. The composition operator is defined to handle the support sets of its two operands independently. The Warshall's algorithm variant uses a recursive helper that processes each element in the support set one at a time.
